title: Server-Side Technology
body:
Interview prep note. See [[Server Side]] and [[Node.js]] for the course-notes versions.

## Core Facts to Know

- The [[Frontend]] runs on the user's machine, inside the browser.
- Frontend code should never hold logic that can't be trusted, because DevTools can read and modify all of it.
- The [[Backend]] runs on their machine(s) and the client never sees the code.
- The [[API]] is the boundary between frontend and backend.
- [[Ruby on Rails]] is an opinionated framework built around [[MVC]].
- The Rails **Model** holds data and business rules and is backed by [[ActiveRecord]].
- ActiveRecord lets you write `Review.where(rating: 5)` instead of hand-written SQL.
- The Rails **View** renders HTML or JSON on the server, before the response is sent.
- The Rails **Controller** receives the parsed request, calls the model, and hands off to the view.
- Rails **Routes** map URL + HTTP method to a controller action.
- A [[Database Migration]] is a versioned, incremental schema change.
- Migrations are run against the database on their machine or in CI.
- Everything in Rails runs on the server, never in the browser.
- A [[SQL]] table is a shelf holding one type of record.
- A row is one record in a table.
- A column is one attribute every record in that table has.
- A [[Primary Key]] uniquely identifies a row.
- A [[Foreign Key]] is a column pointing at another table's primary key.
- Foreign keys are what make a relational database *relational*.
- A [[JOIN]] combines rows from two tables in one query.
- A JOIN executes on the database server, not on the app server.
- A [[Database Index]] makes lookups fast without scanning every row.
- Indexes are stored and maintained on the database server.
- SQL databases (Postgres, [[MySQL]]) enforce a predefined schema.
- [[NoSQL]] databases ([[MongoDB]], DynamoDB) allow flexible, mixed-shape documents.
- The database server is usually a different machine than the app server.

## Core analogy: The restaurant, front-of-house vs. back-of-house

Front-of-house (frontend) is everything the guest directly sees and touches. Back-of-house (backend/server) is the kitchen and the walk-in fridge — invisible to the guest, but what actually produces and stores everything front-of-house presents.

## The split, mapped

| Restaurant concept | Term | Where it runs |
|---|---|---|
| The dining room, menu design, table service | Frontend — [[HTML]]/CSS/[[JavaScript]] | **Your (the user's) machine**, inside the browser — should never hold logic that can't be trusted, since DevTools can read/modify all of it |
| The kitchen, walk-in fridge, inventory ledger, invisible to guests | Backend — business logic, database access, auth checks | **Their machine(s)** — the client never directly sees or touches this code |
| The pass-through window between dining room and kitchen | API | The **boundary** between the two — request travels **your machine → their machine**, response travels back |

## Ruby on Rails, in this analogy

Rails is a fully-equipped, opinionated kitchen — a standard layout (MVC) so any trained chef knows where the knives are.

| Kitchen concept | Rails term | Where it runs |
|---|---|---|
| Recipe plus pantry inventory logic | Model, backed by ActiveRecord (`Review.where(rating: 5)` instead of hand-written SQL) | **Their machine** — the app server process |
| The finished plate's presentation | View — template rendering HTML/JSON | **Their machine**, before the response is sent |
| The line cook deciding which recipe to use and plating the result | Controller | **Their machine** — receives the parsed request, calls the model, hands off to the view |
| The order-taking rulebook mapping requests to line cooks | Routes — URL + method → controller action | **Their machine** — consulted the instant a request arrives |
| A versioned blueprint for renovating storage over time | Migrations — incremental schema changes | Run **on their machine (or CI)** against the database, kept in sync across environments |

The [[Express]] route handlers from COMP 3612 are the same idea in [[Node.js]]: a routing table mapping URL + method to a function that builds a response.

## SQL and database storage, in this analogy

| Kitchen concept | Term | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|
| A shelf holding one type of item | Table (e.g. `reviews`, `products`) | **Their machine** — the database server, often physically separate from the app server |
| One specific item on that shelf | Row | Same — **database server** |
| A labeled attribute every item has | Column | Same |
| A unique inventory tag on every item | Primary key | Same |
| A note on one shelf's item pointing to another shelf's item | Foreign key — what makes it *relational* | Same — enforced by the database engine itself |
| Combining two shelves' info in one trip | JOIN | Executed **on the database server**; the app server just sends the query and receives the combined result |
| A card catalog for fast lookups without checking every item | Index | Stored and maintained **on the database server** |
| Strict predefined shelf layout vs. flexible mixed-shape items | SQL (Postgres, MySQL, schema enforced) vs. NoSQL (MongoDB, DynamoDB, flexible schema) | Both are **database servers**, distinct from and usually on different machines than the app server |

## Tying it back to the role

The stated need is understanding "client-side and server-side web apps in any language" plus nice-to-have Ruby/Rails/SQL. The interview-relevant skill isn't reciting Rails syntax — it's being able to point to *which machine* a given piece of logic runs on, and explain *why* it has to run there rather than the other side of the split.

---
Part of [[Web Interview Prep]].
